title: Spatially informed policies can accelerate green hydrogen demand - Nature Energy
text:
Download PDF

Realized green hydrogen demand lags behind policy targets but could be accelerated by accounting for spatial spillovers, which refer to demand-side interdependencies where adoption by one user encourages further adoption by nearby users. Revising EU green hydrogen policies, including Hydrogen Valleys and European Hydrogen Bank auctions, to better account for these location-specific demand-side patterns could improve their effectiveness.Messages for policy

Demand-side interdependencies arising from spatial spillovers are likely to shape green hydrogen uptake but are largely absent from current EU policy instruments.

Prioritizing regions with strong spillover potential (Rhine–Ruhr, North Sea coast) and industrial sectors (iron and steel, chemicals) could strengthen the impact of hydrogen support policies.

Revising EU Hydrogen Valley calls to require commitments from multiple large-scale offtakers could catalyse regional uptake.

Adding demand or spatial spillover scores to European Hydrogen Bank auctions, or screening projects for strong demand linkages, could improve cost-effectiveness and bid-to-contract conversion rates.

REPowerEU hydrogen corridor investments should be sequenced to prioritize links between multiple industrial offtakers and regions with strong spillover potential.

based on Rumpelnik, C., Zakeri, B. & Surana, K. Nat. Energy https://doi.org/10.1038/s41560-026-02126-2 (2026).The policy problemRealized green hydrogen demand is falling short of policy targets: today, less than 1% of EU hydrogen originates from green sources and only 7% of announced capacity has been completed on schedule. Beyond cost competitiveness, green hydrogen uptake depends on demand-side interdependencies linked to shared infrastructure, supply chains and knowledge exchange. Yet, aside from sectoral mandates for the aviation, shipping and industrial hydrogen sectors, EU policy instruments remain primarily supply-side. EU Hydrogen Valleys, a place-based policy designed to enable regional ecosystems, gives limited consideration to demand (existing valleys target 0.2 Mt demand or 1% of the EU’s 2030 goal). European Hydrogen Bank auctions likewise do not account for demand-side linkages. Current policy instruments are falling short of expectations: amid demand uncertainties, the 2025 European Hydrogen Bank auction awarded only 23% of its €1.2 billion budget. Accelerating hydrogen uptake requires updating and extending these policies based on an improved understanding of demand-side interdependencies.The findingsGreen hydrogen uptake is shaped by spatial spillovers: when one user adopts, others in the area are more likely to follow. The effect of these spillovers grows to more than twenty times their average when cost competitiveness is still low. Spillover potential is highly concentrated in industrial areas of Western–Central Europe (Rhine–Ruhr, North Sea coast) and hard-to-abate industrial sectors (iron and steel, chemicals), presenting clear targets for place- and sector-based policy interventions (Fig. 1). A spatially informed demand-side policy intervention that targets this spillover potential reduces policy costs per kilogram of additional green hydrogen demand by 37–41% (€0.83–0.96) relative to a spatially-neutral baseline, holding size, sector and cost competitiveness constant. This effect persists in a realistic policy setting: adding a 10% spatial criterion to a European Hydrogen Bank-style auction still improves cost-effectiveness by 13–15%. Results may extend to other technologies with value chain interdependencies (such as carbon capture).Fig. 1: Spatial spillover potential among prospective green hydrogen offtakers in Europe.Full size imagea,b, Spatial spillover potential across the EU, measured as local connectivity (hydrogen valleys, a) and connectivity between regions (hydrogen corridors, b). These measures indicate where hydrogen valleys and corridors could emerge through spillovers. Markers show EU-designated hydrogen valleys by scale, and arrows show European Hydrogen Backbone import corridors. Areas with high spillover potential are concentrated in industrial regions but overlap only partly with existing valleys and corridors. c,d, Local patterns in North Rhine-Westphalia and Eastern Austria/Moravia. The 50 highest-scoring offtakers are highlighted, with outlines indicating sector. High-potential clusters are dominated by hard-to-abate industries. Results are based on 14,108 prospective offtakers, with both measures standardized from zero to one. Figure adapted from Rumpelnik, C., Zakeri, B. & Surana, K. Nat. Energy https://doi.org/10.1038/s41560-026-02126-2 (2026).The studyOur study combines an installation-level model of green hydrogen demand diffusion (calibrated on natural gas power generation as a historical analogue) with an original dataset. The dataset provides harmonized geospatial data on production, energy consumption and emissions for 14,108 green hydrogen offtakers — users that could switch from fossil-based to green hydrogen use — in hard-to-abate industrial, transport, power and heating sectors. We then quantify spatial spillover potential using network centrality measures, which capture connectivity between different offtakers. Based on this, we simulate green hydrogen adoption from 2024 to 2100, and compare the cost effectiveness (the cost per additional kilogram of green hydrogen demand) of two policy interventions (one size, sector and cost-controlled, and one mirroring the real-world European Hydrogen Bank setting) to spatially neutral alternatives. We provide results for a range of cost competitiveness and saturation (share of green hydrogen relative to other decarbonization technologies) scenarios.
